question: A patient sustains an open tibial fracture from a road traffic accident. The wound is 6 cm with extensive periosteal stripping and a contaminated wound bed; the bone is adequately covered by soft tissue and there is no vascular injury. Which Gustilo-Anderson grade applies?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Type I: wound <1 cm, clean puncture from inside-out, minimal contamination, simple fracture pattern. This wound is 6 cm and heavily contaminated, ruling out Type I.
Type II: wound 1–10 cm, moderate contamination, adequate soft tissue coverage, no periosteal stripping. This wound has extensive periosteal stripping, which upgrades it beyond Type II.

Correct. Type IIIA: wound >10 cm or extensive soft-tissue damage with periosteal stripping, but adequate bone coverage remains after debridement; any high-energy mechanism with adequate coverage falls here. The 6 cm wound with periosteal stripping and contamination, but adequate bone coverage and no vascular injury, fits IIIA.

Type IIIC: any open fracture with arterial injury requiring repair regardless of wound size. There is no vascular injury in this patient, so IIIC does not apply. Remember: IIIC = vascular injury; limb salvage vs amputation decision is made here.

overallFeedback.feedback: Review Gustilo-Anderson: I (<1 cm, clean), II (1–10 cm, moderate), IIIA (periosteal stripping but bone covered), IIIB (bone exposed, needs flap), IIIC (arterial injury). Periosteal stripping is the key feature distinguishing II from IIIA.

Correct. Gustilo IIIA = extensive soft-tissue damage + periosteal stripping + bone coverage adequate. The key upgrade from II→III is periosteal stripping OR high-energy mechanism. IIIB = inadequate bone coverage needing flap; IIIC = arterial injury.
